/Issued 314 AM MST Tue Nov 17 2026/ 

 - Meteorological Overview:

A period of active and cooler weather conditions begins today as the 
first in series of Pacific upper level troughs continues inland and 
takes on a negative tilt, pivoting a plume of anomalous Pacific 
moisture (PWATS > 200% of normal) across the Northern Rockies
today. Precipitation developing along and west of the continental
divide early this morning will gradually shift east within an 
area of deformation beneath an upper level jet lifting north into 
western Canada through mid-day. Initial precipitation (mainly 
snow) through this morning will be focused across areas from 
northern Lewis and Clark county north through Glacier county, with
accumulating snowfall this morning primarily across Glacier and 
western portions of Pondera county. Mid-level convergence and 
frontogenesis strengthens this afternoon as the deformation axis 
kicks east of the divide, resulting in widespread precipitation 
development along and west of the I-15 corridor this afternoon, 
which gradually shifts eastward through this evening before the 
mid- upper level trough axis ejects out across MT later tonight 
through Wednesday. 

Snow levels currently range from around 4000 ft or less along the 
Rocky Mtn Front to around 7000 ft across SW MT with cooling aloft 
and lowering snow levels shifting east with the upper level front 
and precipitation this afternoon and evening. Snow will increase over 
passes along the continental divide in central/SW MT this afternoon 
with a transition to wet snow occurring at lower elevations along and 
east of I-15 in the late afternoon through early evening period. 
There is still quite a bit of uncertainty in the precise timing of 
the transition to snow for these areas as higher precipitation 
intensity, which is likely to develop under stronger forcing and 
a band of enhanced precipitation early this evening and will 
likely aid in more rapid low-level cooling and a transition to 
wet snow than models are depicting. After midnight, the area of 
steadier precipitation/snow will lift out across eastern portions 
of north-central MT with snow levels also falling to the plains 
there overnight, while some snow lingers in and near the mountains
of central and southwest MT in moist WNW flow behind the trough 
axis into Wednesday morning before ending. 

A cool and unsettled period of weather is maintained as additional 
Pacific energy moves onshore later this week and weekend. Another 
large scale trough/upper low looks to move inland in the Thu/Fri 
period with yet another arriving late in the weekend. Specific 
details are still uncertain with the bulk of the energy from these 
systems looking to track south of the area but potential for 
moisture/precipitation to be drawn north across the area at times
exists. Daytime maximum temperatures in 30s are expected though 
the weekend and any precipitation later this week into the weekend
will likely to be snow. Hoenisch

 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

Overall precipitation/snow amounts have not changed significantly 
and Winter Weather advisories are in place for most of the forecast 
area. In addition to remaining uncertainty in the timing of 
precipitation changing to snow at lower elevations later today, above 
freezing ground temperatures and near freezing air temperatures 
lead to lower than average confidence in snow accumulation amounts 
for most lower elevation locations.  

Some areas to watch for moderate winter weather impacts 
today/tonight include:

Glacier county...Where snow accumulation will come in two rounds 
(this morning and again later this afternoon/evening) and the 
probability for total accumulation of 6 inches or more is as high
as 60-70% at the Alberta border and 30-40% for areas along US-2 
including Cut Bank, Browning and East Glacier. Coldest ground and 
air temperatures exist here with potential for road surface icing
and some localized blowing/drifting snow tonight with the 
development of northwest winds gusting 20-30 mph. 

Continental Divide Passes from Rogers Pass south to Homestake...Where 
periods of moderate to heavy wet snow are likely between 4pm-8pm. 
Enhanced snowfall rates of one half to one inch per hour may occur 
during this time, leading to significant visibility reduction and 
quick snow accumulation on road surfaces.  

The I-15 corridor north of Helena through Great Falls and 
Shelby...Where a N-S band of moderate to embedded heavier precipitation
rates is likely to develop after 4pm and may persist for areas 
from Great Falls north to the border through much of the evening.

snowfall rates along the I-15 corridor may coincide with the
